This project is jointly funded by the Polymers Program in the Division of Materials Research and by the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR).


NON-TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Understanding the dynamics of electronically active polymeric materials is crucial for the development of next-generation foldable and deformable electronic devices. It is also envisioned that in the near future implantable electronic devices could provide unique interfaces between the human body and emerging electronics, thus restoring lost human function, such as hearing, vision, and bodily movement.  However, there are no established design roles to understand, control, and predict the softness and pliability of such new electronically active materials. This project aims to address this challenge by developing fundamental new knowledge on the dynamics of polymer macromolecules and thus provide a pathway to make ultra-soft electronics that can enable the next generation of soft electronic devices for future wearables and implants.  The researchers at the University of Southern Mississippi will develop, test, and validate new electronically active polymers using special instrumentation and develop new models to predict and control their softness.   The research will include development of design rules to achieve tunable control of the electronic and mechanical properties of semiconducting polymers by measuring, understanding, and manipulating their mechanical properties and molecular entanglement behavior.

In addition to research involvement of graduate and undergraduate students, the educational effort of the project would implement an integrated and curiosity-driven virtual and in-person education platform on polymeric and optoelectronic materials to local K-12 students, including school districts comprising a majority of underrepresented students. Broader impacts will also include a focused Southern U.S. X-ray/neutron scattering workshop to bring new scientific techniques to the local scientific community.


TECHNICAL SUMMARY 

Organic semiconductors based on conjugated polymers exhibit unique optoelectronic properties and have been widely applied in a broad range of applications for efficient lighting, health care, energy harvesting, and storage. Despite promising advances in their optoelectrical properties, the ability to predict and control thermomechanical properties is lagging behind. Thus, the overall goal of this project is to develop new design rules to achieve tunable control of the electronic and mechanical properties of conjugated polymers by measuring, understanding, and manipulating their glass transition temperature as well as their molecular entanglement behavior. Researchers at the University of Southern Mississippi will target the following goals:  1) accurately determine the glass transition temperature for conjugated polymers and its influence on the mechanical properties in both device-relevant thin-film confined states and bulk state;   2) illustrate the design rules for engineering highly entangled polymer chains to understand the role entangled semi-rigid chains have on final fracture behavior of free-standing thin films under confinement;  and  3) understand the deformation mechanism of semi-rigid conjugated polymers using multimodal in-situ spectroscopy and scattering techniques, and thus guide the design of future deformable electronics.  The fundamental knowledge gained through this project will lead to precise control of the thermomechanical properties of conjugated polymers, thus contributing to the development of future soft robotics, implantable health care, and robust energy harvesting devices.

abstractText:
The Mississippi Alliance for Women in Computing (MAWC) project will identify factors that influence and motivate female students and female African American students in Mississippi to enroll and persist in an undergraduate engineering- or science-based computing major.  There is a particular need for programming that is inclusive of women and women of color who are from the southern region of the United States. These students typically have less access to extracurricular activities that encourage computing, and are less likely to visualize themselves in a computing major or career. This proposed research is to help girls to know that computer science exists and what jobs in computer science are available with a degree in computer science. A rich environment exists in Mississippi for an alliance focused on building co-curricular and mentorship opportunities.  A scalable pipeline model, expandable to a Southern Alliance for Women in Computing (SAWC), will be developed with three major objectives: to attract women and women of color to computing, to improve retention rates of women in undergraduate computing majors, and to help postsecondary women make the transition to the computing workforce. Activities to support these objectives include: scaling the National Center for Women and Information Technology Aspirations in Computing award program in Mississippi, expanding scholarships for Aspirations winners, expanding student-led computing outreach programs, establishing a Mississippi Black Girls Code chapter, informing and collaborating with the Computer Science for Mississippi initiative, creating a summer bridge and living-learning community for women in computing majors, and increasing professional development opportunities for women in computing through conferences, lunch and learn meetings, job shadowing, and internships.
 
The project will analyze whether the co-curricular activities of MAWC lead to computing self-efficacy and ultimately female students selecting to pursue and persist in computing majors and careers.  In order to understand student participation and efficacy changes, data collection for this research will be through demographic and background surveys administered to women entering an undergraduate engineering- or science-based computing major at a university in Mississippi and student surveys and evaluations in MAWC-sponsored programs.  Using discriminate analysis methods, specific research questions to be addressed are: 1) Which pre-collegiate experiences influenced them to enroll, 2) Which stakeholders influenced these girls in their decision-making process, and 3) What programs are effective in impacting their persistence in the major. Predictor variables for each respective research question are: pre-collegiate experiences, stakeholders, and programs. Outcome variables are: (a) a female undergraduate student with no involvement with MAWC programming, (b) MAWC activity participant, or (c) a MAWC participant having graduated with a bachelor?s degree in a STEM major. Results will complement published longitudinal research on the gendered and raced dimensions of computing literacy acquisition in Mississippi as well as research on effective CS role model programming.

Project Outcomes Summary

The NSF INCLUDES Mississippi Alliance for Women in Computing (MSAWC) project was designed to build and leverage relationships throughout the state of Mississippi to increase participation of women in computing by improving recruitment and retention rates of women in undergraduate computing majors and helping post-secondary women make a transition to the computing workforce. Activities designed to engage females with computing, emphasizing computational thinking and cybersecurity knowledge and awareness, and to illuminate a pathway forward were hosted and facilitated through MSAWC partnerships. MSAWC outcomes informed formal K-12 computer science education, documented the importance of mentoring and tutoring services in retention of computing undergraduate students, and connected workforce development entities with higher ed to provide alternative pathways to computing education and the higher wage jobs that result from that skills development. Through connecting people in Mississippi to stakeholders from outside the state, MSAWC conversations sparked ideas that resulted in a larger consortium to bring computer science and cybersecurity education to under-represented minority and female students throughout the United States and a non-profit to provide wrap-around services that help women persist in undergraduate computing majors.

Data Collection through MSAWC activities, facilitated at the host institution, found that both tutoring and counseling services were the most influential among other campus student services in helping participants persist in a computing major. Summer outreach computing program participation, student interest in technology, access to high school engineering/computing courses, and familial and other mentors were all influential in the choice to select a computing major as an entering undergraduate student. 

Significant Outcomes of MSAWC partnerships and collaborations

  •  Mississippi Coding Academies (MCA): MCA provides workforce development training, at no cost to participants, for rapid upskilling into higher wage technical jobs such as full stack software development, technology support, and cybersecurity. The non-profit MCA has collaborative governance with InnovateMS, The University of Southern Mississippi, Mississippi State University (MSU), and other industry, government, and non-profit stakeholders through its Board of Directors. Three-fourth of the trainees that have completed the program are from an under-represented minority group and around one-fourth are female. MCA has also launched cybersecurity workforce training to increase career pathway opportunities and enable Mississippians to upskill and reskill for the future of work that includes a growing cybersecurity defense sector.
  • Attract-Inspire-Mentor Computer Science (CS) Teacher Professional Development (PD): This transdisciplinary PD approach was developed by Bagley College of Engineering and College of Educator researchers at MSU with the following goals: a) Attract teachers to CS learning by meeting them where they are in the comfort of their current content areas, enabling them to develop self-efficacy with computing as an extension of their current areas of expertise. b) Inspire teachers to pursue the use of computing concepts in their classrooms, with follow on activities that enable them to showcase their work and that of their students c) Mentor teachers by providing opportunity for knowledge sharing and mentoring among teachers, industry, and college/university faculty. A 3-hour credit course, "Computing and Cyber Security Integration in the Classroom,” for in-service teachers based on Attract-Inspire-Mentor was designed at the undergraduate/graduate level and is offered at Mississippi State University. In August 2019, The Mississippi State Board of Education approved a 12-hour pre-service computer science endorsement for Grades K-8 and an 18-hour supplemental endorsement for Grades 7-12. "Computing and Cyber Security Integration in the Classroom" was selected to be part of the grades 7-12 endorsement curriculum at MSU.
  • Bulldog Bytes K-12 Student Outreach Program: Established at Mississippi State University, this program introduced over 1000 K-12 learners to computing and cybersecurity. Activities implemented in Bulldog Bytes have later been adopted in classrooms in Mississippi. These include the use of robots to teach coding and an innovative introduction of algorithmic thinking to K-12 students through dance.
  • The CS-JROTC Demonstration Project idea was sparked at the MSAWC initial kick-off meeting in 2017. To close the gap in schools offering CS coursework, CSForAll, with NSF funding, provided leadership for this project with the US Airforce JROTC Headquarters, and an Advisory Consortium of industry and other stakeholders. Teachers at JROTC schools were provided professional development for CS teaching, and a summer cyber academy for cadets was piloted in summer 2020 (hosted in Mississippi) and scaled to other host sites in 2021.
  • MSAWC enabled an expansion of and deepening of relationships both within and outside the state of Mississippi. One example and resulting outcome is the Last Mile Education Fund. Led by a trusted partner, and inspired by a participant in MSAWC activities, the Last Mile Education Fund was founded to help women in computing majors persist to graduation by helping them to overcome financial obstacles that are a barrier to reaching graduation.

With funding from the Macromolecular, Supramolecular and Nanochemistry Program of the Chemistry Division, Professors Lei Fang of Texas A&M University and Xiaodan Gu of University of Southern Mississippi are investigating how chain flexibility influences the physical properties of conjugated ladder polymers.  Conjugated polymers are a unique class of non-metallic polymers with semiconducting properties resembling that of the chemical element silicon.  These long chain carbon-based molecules can become conductive when external voltage is applied (like in transistors) or light shines on them (like in photovoltaic cells).  Conjugated polymers are extensively used in solar cells, LED screens and other applications that utilize the conversion of electricity to light.  Ladder polymers, on the other hand, are a type of double stranded polymers with the connectivity of a ladder.  This is achieved by interconnecting repeating units along the main polymer chain by four chemical bonds, instead of the two bonds typically seen in conventional plastics.  In this research, conjugated ladder polymers with varied structural features are synthesized.  Control polymers are prepared with deliberately introduced backbone defects that consist of small molecules.  Detailed studies are then conducted to correlate backbone composition and length with the flexibility of the polymer chains.  These studies are enabled by employing neutron and light scattering techniques which provide accuracy at lengths ranging from sub 1 nanometer (1/100,000 of human hair diameter) to well beyond 10 micrometers (the width of cotton fiber).  Correlations established as a result of this work may provide knowledge that could lead to the development of materials with better optical and electronic performance.  Educational innovation tackles the problems associated with outdated contents in undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory courses.  The newly designed “Nobel Prize Reactions” are first implemented at both universities and then disseminated at national and international scales.  Outreach activities expose undergraduate and high school students to modern chemical research.  This work is specifically designed to benefit a large number of underrepresented minorities and economically disadvantaged students in Mississippi.

The primary goal of this research is to establish the fundamental correlations between backbone constitution and the chain rigidity for rigid ladder conjugated polymers.  The research is conducted through the design and synthesis of model ladder polymers with varied structural features, and controls with deliberately introduced backbone defects, followed by quantitative evaluation of their chain persistence length and correlation with structural features.  Chain rigidity of the ladder polymer models and controls is quantified using combined modern characterization tools with an emphasis on neutron and light scattering.  Studies are also performed to understand the influence of chain bending energy on persistent length for ladder polymers.  Comprehensive structural-rigidity correlation through iterative design-synthesis-measurement-design cycles is established.  Results associated with this award have the potential to advance knowledge on how the chain rigidity (or flexibility) determines the fundamental properties and practical applications of a wide range of polymers.

projectOutComesReport:
This project aims to study an important knowledge gap in polymer science: how stiff is the chain of macromolecules that feature two strands of bonds on the backbone. These polymers are referred to as “ladder polymers”. Most polymers studied in the past century are macromolecular chains consisting of only one strand of bonds. The presence of two strands of bonds in ladder polymers is anticipated to render the polymer chain significantly more rigid due to the restriction of molecular motion. Such a distinct fundamental property is expected to impart unique properties into ladder polymers that are not accessible in conventional polymer materials. This way, new polymeric materials with unprecedented yet unique functions can be developed for advanced applications including polymer electronics, soft robotics, and smart stimuli-responsive materials.

In order to achieve the fundamental understanding of the chain stiffness of ladder polymers, two research groups – Lei Fang's team at Texas A&M University and Xiaodan Gu's team at the University of Southern Mississippi – teamed up to tackle this challenge. Dr. Fang's group synthesized a series of model ladder polymers that are free of single-stranded defects on the chain to serve as the model for the aforementioned investigation. Dr. Gu's group utilized light and neutron scattering techniques to measure the shape of the macromolecular chains and thereby quantify the stiffness of these chains in solution.

Interestingly, an unexpected challenge was encountered during the project. The synthesized ladder polymers were found to be aggregating in solution, although they appeared to be dissolved. The team investigated the aggregation behavior of the polymer and found that such favorable aggregation is formed as a result of the thermodynamics of the intrinsically restricted backbone shape deformation.

In order to tackle this issue, the team designed a next-generation ladder polymer that does not aggregate in solution. The idea is to install bulky molecular groups on the side of the backbone of ladder polymer chains. The bulky groups prevent the chain from stacking with one another due to steric repulsion. Meanwhile, the bulky groups induce pressure on the backbone itself so that it can bend slightly and thereby makes aggregation less probable.

The synthesis of this second-generation ladder polymer was successful. By utilizing light scattering and neutron scattering techniques, the team was able to determine that the polymer chains are indeed fully dissolved in solution without notable aggregation. This result allowed the team to measure and quantify the chain stiffness of the resulting non-aggregating ladder polymers. Interestingly, our result demonstrated that the chain stiffness of these double-stranded polymers is similar to that of single-stranded macromolecular chains with similar structures. This result is intriguing, considering the anticipated higher rigidity of ladder polymers. There are two possible reasons for the unexpected high flexibility: 1. Ladder polymers are only stiff at a small length scale (likely < 2 nm); at a larger length scale, slight bending and twisting motion can accumulate and cause major deformation of the polymer chain. 2. The bulky side-groups installed on the ladder polymer backbone induce bending motion of the backbone and hence promote flexibility of the entire polymer chain.

This interesting finding from this project sheds light on the intrinsic polymer physics of double-stranded polymer chains in a quantitative manner. The results here are critical for our future design of polymer structures for applications that require local stiffness of the polymer chain while overall chain flexibility is needed. For example, such property would be ideal for electrically conductive polymers that also possess the high mechanical toughness and strength of plastics.

In tandem with the research initiatives, the team devoted considerable effort to educational outreach and innovation. A highlight of this endeavor was the design and implementation of a series of organic chemistry laboratory experiments for sophomore-level students. These experiments, inspired by Nobel Prize-winning chemical reactions, provided over 100 undergraduates with the opportunity to engage directly with cutting-edge chemical advances. This practical exposure not only enhanced their learning experience but also aimed to inspire a new generation of scientists by demonstrating the relevance and excitement of frontier research in chemistry. The educational impact of this initiative is expected to extend beyond the laboratory, fostering critical thinking and a deeper understanding of materials science among students.

Light-based microscopes are indispensable to the advancement of many scientific fields. Lamentably, there is a lower limit to the size of objects that can be observed due to physics of light itself. This barrier impedes investigation of minuscule objects. Fortunately, recent advances have helped overcome this hurdle, yielding “super-resolution” microscopes. The specific super-resolution technology acquired by this award is well-suited for imaging dynamic objects like those in cells as well as nanoparticles created in the laboratory.   Projects that will take advantage of the microscope include: material scientists studying assembly of high performance plastic-like materials, cell biologists and biochemists investigating cell components important in Alzheimer’s and genetic tools, and microbiologists that examine bacterial community structures involved in infection and plant-soil interactions. Availability of the super-resolution microscope will provide opportunities for training in cutting-edge imaging for faculty and students throughout Mississippi. Emphasis will be placed on involving underserved communities and faculty at small colleges and universities 

This proposal requests a Leica Stimulated Emission Depletion 3X super resolution microscopy component. The system enables imaging of nano-scale objects smaller than the diffraction limit of light without the need for specialized fluorophores, intense laser exposure, and heavy computational processing of data. Thus, acquisition of the component will benefit numerous projects at the host institute as well as other academic research in the region. It will integrate with an existing confocal microscope housed and maintained in an imaging core facility on the University of Southern Mississippi Hattiesburg campus. The core is a multi-user facility that provides access, consultation, training, and technical support free of charge to Mississippi academic scientists. The module will support the research and education missions of the core facility along with projects supported by multi-institute consortia aimed at engineering novel spectral properties in organic compounds. Together this makes the system a highly accessible instrument, offering a cutting-edge imaging mode to even the most resource limited researchers, while synergistically empowering statewide programs to advance their research programs and education missions.

Light-based microscopes are indispensable to the advancement of many scientific fields. Lamentably, there is a lower limit to the size of objects that can be observed due to physics of light itself. This barrier impedes investigation of the tiniest of objects, which are important to understand for the study of life and material sciences. Fortunately, recent advances have vaulted over this hurdle, giving scientists the tool of "super-resolution" microscopes. The instrument acquired by this award is a specific type of super-resolution microscope that is well-suited for imaging dynamic objects in motion. This includes parts of cells and nanoparticles created in the laboratory. Due to the numerous uses of such a microscope a diverse group of scientists at the University of Southern Mississippi (USM) came together to request this microscope from the National Science Foundation. 

 

Even though the microscope was installed only five month ago as of this writing, many research projects have already taken advantage of its capabilities. Material scientists studying nanoparticles have used it to see interaction of their particles with cells. Biochemists have used the microscope to study the formation of substances that lead to progression of Alzheimer's. Importantly, access to this advanced microscope has led to initiation of research projects at the host institute, USM, that were not possible before. This is evident from grants submitted by faculty that feature the microscope?s capabilities in experimental plans. These projects include studying how ticks feed, and the behavior of immune cells that contribute to allergic reaction. Additional ongoing projects that would not otherwise be possible without the microscope are the study of polymer diffusion, study morphologies of imprinted polymers on electrodes, doping of conjugated polymers, and structures formed by coronaviruses like SARS-CoV-2 inside cells. 

 

In addition to the benefit to research at the host institute, faculty at other universities and colleges in the state have also used the microscope. Chemists from the University of Mississippi have collaborated with cell biologists at USM to study cell-chemical interactions. Access to the microscope's capabilities also benefited a project at the Mississippi University for Women being featured in a grant application from a faculty at this school. Further benefit to research programs are expected. The microscope is advertised as a resource through the two largest research consortiums in the state. The first is the MS INBRE network, a NIH funded program that provides infrastructure for scientific research in Mississippi. Through this program free access is offered to all researchers either through training so researchers can use the microscope themselves or as a service where MS INBRE personnel will take pictures of samples as a service. The other project is the Center for Emergent Optoelectronics (CEMOS), an EPSCoR track I project that brings together Mississippi's most capable researchers for a collaborative project. Thus by advertising through both program the full gamut of researchers, both those at small schools and large, research active schools will be reached and become potential users.

 

Access to the microscope also offers training opportunity for students in Mississippi. Shortly after installation of the microscope, faculty held workshops for training in super resolution as well as other microscope technologies. The workshop had over 50 attendees, including students from HBCUs, such Jackson State University and Alcorn State University. In addition to providing training opportunities, the microscope was also featured on the local news for counties around USM. Communication with the public that USM possesses cutting edge technology, greatly benefits USM with recruiting the best local students.

abstractText:
To meet the ever-growing energy need for powering numerous wireless devices in applications of smart city, precision agriculture, and public safety, energy harvesting is emerging as a promising alternative to traditional power grids and batteries. Through scavenging radio energy from the surrounding environment, the radio frequency (RF) energy harvesting device can run semi-perpetually without a battery replacement. The energy harvesting feature, however, raises unique vulnerabilities in RF energy harvesting wireless networks. The investigator identifies a radically new threat model, called malicious energy attack: the adversary energy source threatens the information security by intentionally charging specific nodes to manipulate routing paths in the network layer. This project explores the non-linearity in energy harvesting systems and investigates reinforcement learning-enabled energy attack and defense mechanisms. It aims to develop efficient and secure communications for RF energy harvesting wireless networks. The project is expected to support development of sustainable and secure wireless networks, thereby leading to a broad impact on industrial sectors relying on energy harvesting techniques. The material generated from this project will be integrated into multiple courses on computer security and wireless networks.
 
This project is organized around two research topics. The first topic develops offline and online optimal data transmission strategies based on a new nonlinear recursive energy harvesting model that considers the energy clamp phenomenon caused by dynamic RF environment, the nonlinear charging of the battery, and the nonlinear harvesting circuits. The second topic proposes a reinforcement learning-enabled intelligent energy attack method, where the adversary energy source can intelligently charge and control the energy level of each infected node based on the partial information of the traffic distribution in the network. Meanwhile, two defense mechanisms are developed to protect RF energy harvesting wireless networks from malicious energy attacks. In performing the above tasks, this research will build an RF energy harvesting wireless network testbed to facilitate radical breakthroughs over the practical design of models, algorithms, and protocols in forked projects.

This project is jointly funded by CISE CCF and the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR).

abstractText:
People have a powerful need to interact with each other. They also have strong desires to avoid disease.  Social distancing is the primary behavioral method to stop disease from spreading.  Yet, social distancing goes against the natural desire for social interactions. The tension between those dual motives can cause psychological distress, and may lead people to violate restrictions on face-to-face contact in their effort to relieve stress and loneliness. This is especially likely for people who do not have access to highly immersive forms of virtual socialization, such as internet-based video calls that let people see friends and family. It may also apply more often for older adults (who are most vulnerable to COVID-19) because of less familiarity with technology-based interaction platforms.  By better understanding how people resolve the tension between the need to interact with others and the desire to avoid disease, this project will inform the development of public health interventions aimed at curbing the spread of disease.

This project contrasts the need to affiliate with the desire to avoid disease.  One aim is to inform the development of interventions designed to avoid loneliness while engaging in social distancing.  Study 1 collects data from the same participants across multiple days. Measures of loneliness, concerns with contracting an illness, and amounts and types of social interactions will be collected. The research tests the hypothesis that participants with limited access to virtual social interactions (e.g., those with limited financial means, the elderly) will feel most lonely and report decreased concerns about disease, which will be associated with more frequent violations of social distancing behaviors. Study 2 experimentally manipulates feelings of inclusion versus exclusion to test for effects of social isolation and for the concern of contracting the disease.  Both studies are based on large and representative samples of U.S. residents to ensure the findings are applicable across different age ranges, geographical regions, and socioeconomic groups within the country.  The research elucidates how various psychological processes work against each other and in interaction to ultimately influence social behavior.  The research further investigates how people can safely satisfy their motives to affiliate without sacrificing safety.  The long-term goal is to inform the development of interventions that may be developed to promote appropriate behavioral responses during the current and future pandemics.

projectOutComesReport:
The COVID-19 pandemic created a public health crisis that highlighted the need to better understand how people manage their need for social affiliation and their desire to avoid contagious disease. The current program of research considered how a pervasive need to belong may come into conflict with necessary public health initiatives that serve to mitigate the spread of disease through interpersonal contact by limiting social interactions. We conducted two studies investigating how to leverage this interplay to identify individual differences most predictive of adhering to social distancing guidelines despite the potential costs associated with social isolation, and to use these findings to inform a subsequent intervention to encourage COVID-19 social distances recommendations. Study 1 recruited from a nationally representative sample, wherein we assessed individual differences in need to belong and perceived vulnerability to disease while considering the extent individuals adhered to social distancing guidelines during Summer 2020. We additionally considered participants? consumption of technology, which we argued would provide means through which individuals could satisfy their need to belong through virtual interactions (e.g., Zoom calls). Results indicated dispositionally heightened motivations to avoid disease were predictive of greater adherence to social distancing guidelines, whereas a chronically heightened need to belong was associated with less adherence to guidelines. Subsequent analyses further suggested that technology was unexpectedly associated with less adherence to these guidelines despite it similarly satisfying belonging needs.

 These results suggest that the pervasiveness of affiliative needs impedes adherence to public health initiatives, even when the threat of disease exposure is similarly exacerbated. Technologically mediated interactions further appeared to have merely whetted the appetites of respondents, suggesting technology by itself may not be an optimal intervention to foster adherence to health initiatives. Our second study sought to consider more personalized interactions with technology in their capability to assuage the negative effects of isolation. We specifically considered social surrogacy as a more personalized use, or a vicarious relationship individuals have with media experiences. In this study, we fostered either feelings of inclusion or exclusion among adults before tasking them to think about a favorite television show (versus other social experiences). This was followed by participants indicating their interest in adhering to social distancing guidelines. We found no evidence that social surrogacy is capable of fostering adherence to social distancing guidelines, although we found that older adults in our sample reported greater interest in deviating from these guidelines when following both an exclusionary experience and reminders of their favorite television program. Taken together, these findings demonstrate current technology available to satisfy social needs virtually seem insufficient in their ability to satisfying humans? need to belong in preventing interest in risky behavior.  Future work in this area should consider ways in which technology-mediated social interaction can better mirror physically-present interactions to ensure better satisfaction of social needs, particularly during public health crises associated with the outbreak of highly contagious pathogens.

 Results contribute to our intellectual merit goals for this project by providing evidence for how two motivational systems in humans compete with each other, resulting in a trade-off in satisfying one motive versus another. This trade-off broadly positions our work within current discussions of life history theory that focus on how humans weigh the costs and benefits of their behavior in satisfying a specific motive at the expense of others. This work additionally clarifies previous findings from this research team demonstrating a general interest in people to incur the costs of disease transmission in the service of belonging to a group. Further consideration for the broader implications of our findings focuses on the interplay between motivation and technology, particularly as it relates to the development of technology that could more adequately mirror social interactions. Such development could lead to technology that encourages adherence to public health initiatives that could prevent disease transmission more easily due to its ability to satisfy a sense of belonging similarly to human interaction. Greater adherence would necessarily increase the likelihood of public health initiatives having greater success in controlling disease spread. Additionally, this work saw the involvement of a diverse team of researchers to meet NSF goals to foster inclusivity in scientific endeavors; our grant saw several mentees from underrepresented backgrounds (e.g., women, first-generation college students, international students) participate in this process, resulting in peer-reviewed publications.

This Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) site award to The University of Southern Mississippi, located in Hattiesburg, MS, supports the training of 10 students for 10 weeks during the summers of 2020-2022. In this program, supported by the Division of Chemistry in the Mathematical and Physical Sciences Directorate and the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR), undergraduate participants pursue research projects in chemistry and biochemistry. Participants also take part in a professional development and ethics training program, with a focus on lab safety, oral communication, scientific writing, and preparation for graduate school or industrial careers. Through independent research projects, workshops, and panel discussions, the participants are prepared for advanced degrees and/or industrial careers in STEM. 
 
The students undertake individual projects encompassing all fields of chemistry and biochemistry with a common theme of utilizing non-covalent interactions. These projects include assembly of macromolecules and proteins, ultra-sensitive and quantitative detection, and asymmetric synthesis of bioactive molecules and their applications in biochemistry. To increase diversity in the STEM pipeline, this site recruits underrepresented student groups, women, and first-generation college students from historically black colleges and universities, women's universities, and community colleges in the state of Mississippi. This program provides intensive research and professional training to undergraduate students that do not have access to formal scientific research labs, increasing their retention in STEM career fields.

The objective of this program was to inspire and prepare undergraduate students for scientific careers by providing an immersive summer research experience in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at The University of Southern Mississippi (USM). Although the program was delayed by one year due to COVID-19, between 2021 and 2024 we fully or partially supported 40 students selected from 349 applications. Our REU participants represented a wide range of backgrounds, coming from 38 unique institutions across 23 states. Importantly, 34 of the 40 students (85%) attended institutions without a PhD program in chemistry or related fields, highlighting the program’s success in broadening access to state-of-the-art research opportunities for students who may otherwise have limited exposure. 

During the summer, students worked closely with faculty and graduate mentors to develop critical research skills in experimental design, data analysis, scientific instrumentation, and modern laboratory techniques. Research projects spanned all five core areas of chemistry—analytical, biochemistry, inorganic, organic, and physical chemistry—unified by the central theme of non-covalent interactions and their role in shaping molecular and material properties. Beyond laboratory training, students participated in professional development workshops on research ethics, scientific communication, computing and modeling, graduate school applications, and career pathways in chemistry and biochemistry. The program culminated with poster and oral presentations, and many students went on to present their work at national venues. Eight participants presented at ACS national meetings, and two co-authored peer-reviewed publications.

Assessment results indicate that this integrated research and training experience significantly enhanced students’ preparation for future careers in science. Among the 40 REU alumni, 21 (53%) have matriculated into graduate school and 9 (23%) have entered the STEM workforce, demonstrating the program’s sustained contribution to the U.S. STEM workforce developments.

This Site is jointly funded by the Divisions of Chemistry and Materials Research in the Mathematical and Physical Sciences (MPS) Directorate.

NON-TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION: This REU Site brings together undergraduate students from across the country to perform research aimed at critical societal needs with faculty and students in the state-of-the-art Polymer Science and Engineering Research Center. REU students, recruited from primarily undergraduate institutions, historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs), and community colleges, work in interdisciplinary research teams and receive training in polymer science and engineering, science communication, sustainability, and life-cycle analysis during the ten-week summer program. Students participate in field trips to local industry, engage in outreach for elementary students, and prepare abstracts for presentation of their research at national conferences. This site helps develop the pipeline of science and engineering researchers with the skills to address the grand challenges of the 21st century while advancing fundamental research to support applications such as recyclable composites for aerospace and automotive sectors, on-demand degradable polymers for packaging, polymers from renewable feedstocks for drug delivery, polymeric solar cells, and flexible printed electronics. Most participants pursue graduate degrees in science and engineering after completing the summer program and are ultimately employed in research and development in industry, national laboratories, or academia. 

TECHNICAL DETAILS: The research objective of the REU site is to develop sustainable approaches to materials development to meet critical societal needs while improving utilization of energy and raw materials. Undergraduate student researchers are engaged in fundamental materials research efforts that span the complex, interdisciplinary facets of materials sustainability, including design of materials for recyclability and degradability, synthesis of polymers from renewable feedstocks, enhancing process efficiency, and designing polymers for renewable energy applications, while gaining the tools to assess the environmental impact of new material development. The research is organized in three themes: (1) Design for Recyclability and Degradability (2) Sustainable Polymers: (Bio) Renewable Feedstocks and Resource-Efficient Processing and (3) Materials for Sustainable Energy. Students are trained in state-of-the-art research facilities, including recently acquired X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) - wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS), and advanced imaging instrumentation, and gain interdisciplinary research skills through collaborative efforts with polymer computational, synthesis, analysis, and processing experts.

projectOutComesReport:
The REU Site: Polymer Innovation for a Sustainable Future (REU) at the School of Polymer Science and Engineering at The University of Southern Mississippi (USM) engaged 52 undergraduate students from 33 different colleges and universities across the country in a ten-week program of summer research and training designed to equip them with the interdisciplinary research and teamwork skills necessary to address the complex challenges of the 21st century. Over the summers of 2020 – 2023, participants engaged in a ten-week integrated research and education program exploring fundamental research projects that span the complex, interdisciplinary facets of materials sustainability, including polymer synthesis from renewable sources, materials with enhanced properties and lifetime, and materials to improve utilization of natural resources (Figs 1, 2). Strengthening the theme of sustainability, students acquired skills and tools to assess the environmental impact of new material development and were encouraged to consider these aspects at each stage of their research projects. To address our objectives of broadening participation, 28 of the 52 participants were from primarily undergraduate institutions or HBCUs, half were from freshman or sophomore year, twenty-eight were women, and thirteen were underrepresented minorities. In addition to spending 40 hours per week in the laboratory with graduate students and faculty advisors, REU students participated in foundational courses in polymer science and engineering, communication skills training, field trips to local industry, career exploration, and seminars by graduate students and visiting scientists (Fig. 3).  The students practiced and developed effective scientific communication skills by providing two oral presentations and a final poster presentation at the MS IDeA/EPSCoR conference, which brought together students from across the state performing research funded by NIH and NSF (Fig 4).  REU participants in each cohort worked on engaging the next generation of scientists and engineers by facilitating outreach events for K-12 students participating in the local urban summer camp that featured hands-on polymer science activities (Fig 5).  The research efforts of the participants resulted in nine refereed publications, 22 presentations at national meetings, and 25 presentations at regional conferences with REU co-authors (Fig 6).  100% of the REUs are on track to graduate with STEM degrees, and of those who have graduates, 78% have enrolled in STEM graduate programs.  These results demonstrate the impact of the REU Site on building an educated workforce to address the grand challenges of science and engineering in our nation.
